newsitem.title: UK: Stocks low but rice price under pressure - FAO.
newsitem.headline: Stocks low but rice price under pressure - FAO.

text.p: World rice prices are coming under pressure as exporters compete in a smaller market after a bumper Asian 1996 crop, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said on Thursday.
The FAO is also expecting a reduced decline in global rice stocks at the end of the 1997 marketing year of 0.9 million tonnes to 52 million tonnes.
Last month FAO had forecast these stocks sliding to 48.9 million tonnes but now Chinese and Indian crops appear much better.
Despite violent storms and floods in the first half of the year, China's crop was largely unscathed and FAO said its early harvest showed a sharp increase from last year.

Generally Asian imports in 1997 will be substantially lower with the Philippines importing only a fraction of the one million tonnes imported in 1996, FAO said in its Rice Situation Update. But Indonesia may remain a substantial importer in 1997.
The 1996 world crop is forecast at 565.4 million tonnes, up from 555.1 million tonnes in 1995. Asia's crop is forecast at a record 517 million after 506.7 million in 1995.
Last month prices for nearly all types of rice slid and FAO's price index for all rice dipped two points to 134 or its lowest for over a year.

FAO is forecasting a four percent fall in 1997 world rice trade to 18.2 million tonnes as better crops erode import demand although the likely carry-over of Japan's import commitment under the World Trade Oreganization (WTO) may provide some support in early 1997.
FAO put world rice trade in 1996 at 18.9 million tonnes down one million from 1995.

FAO's global stock forecast covers aggregate stocks at the end of national marketing years. At end 1997 15.1 million tonnes is expected to be held in China, Pakistan, Thailand, the U.S. and Vietnam -- the world's five main traditional exporters.
Despite the improvement in supplies, FAO said several important importers remain very short of rice with large parts of the North Korean and Iraqi populations at nutritional risk.
But FAO has cut its estimate of imports to both countries as Iraq still lacks UN permission to buy food for oil and N Korea has received a much less food aid in the form of rice.
